meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It is well enough that people of the nation do not understand our banking and monetary system, for if they did, I believe there would be a revolution before tomorrow morning'?
meta.ogDescription: Henry Ford never wrote it. Earliest documented text: a 1937 Congressional Record paraphrase by Rep. Charles Binderup. Later reassigned to Andrew Jackson.

answer.label: Not Henry Ford — a congressman’s 1937 paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: The wording is first documented not in anything Henry Ford wrote or said, but in a speech by Rep. Charles G. Binderup of Nebraska on the floor of the U.S. House on 19 March 1937, where he introduced it with the words “It was Henry Ford who said, in substance, this” — flagging it as his own paraphrase rather than a quotation. No interview, book, letter or speech of Ford’s has ever been produced containing the line, and the version shared today is not even Binderup’s wording but a later, smoother rewrite of it.

source.heading: The earliest documented text

docMeta.dd: Introduced as “in substance” — a paraphrase, not a quotation

source.excerpt:
I wish I could shout this from the mountaintop until the people of our great Nation might know and understand. I assure you that there would then be a change before morning if the people only knew.

It was Henry Ford who said, in substance, this: “It is perhaps well enough that the people of the Nation do not know or understand our banking and monetary system, for if they did I believe there would be a revolution before tomorrow morning.”
trail: The oldest known text of the saying is not Ford’s. It appears in Rep. Charles Binderup’s 19 March 1937 speech to the U.S. House, printed at page 2528 of the Congressional Record ↗, introduced with the words “It was Henry Ford who said, in substance, this.”
Wikiquote places the line in its Misattributed section for Henry Ford ↗, noting that the “in substance” preface marks it as a paraphrase rather than an actual quote.

Quotation researchers on the American Dialect Society list found only indirect, ever-changing versions from 1938 onward — and none in the Yale Book of Quotations or the Oxford Dictionary of Quotations ↗. Ford was alive until 1947, and never appears to have confirmed the line.

A full-text search of Ford’s own My Life and Work (1922) ↗ turns up no “revolution before tomorrow morning.” Its money chapter instead begins: “My objection to bankers has nothing to do with personalities. I am not against bankers as such.”
source.excerptNote: Two things are worth noticing. First, Binderup’s own sentence immediately before — “there would then be a change before morning if the people only knew” — runs so close to the line he then hands to Ford that it is hard to see where his rhetoric ends and Ford’s supposed words begin. Second, this 1937 text is not the wording that circulates today: the popular version drops “perhaps,” drops “know or,” and changes “the people of the Nation” to “people of the nation.”
source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for the wording people share today, because that wording has no identified author and no identified first publication — it is a drifted rewrite of a paraphrase. The one text that is firmly dated, Binderup’s different sentence, appeared in the Congressional Record for 19 March 1937, a U.S. Government Printing Office publication. Ford’s actual writing on banking is in My Life and Work (Doubleday, Page & Co., 1922), which is in the public domain and freely readable at Project Gutenberg.

author.name: Charles G. Binderup
author.kicker: The man who put the words on the record
author.heading: Who actually spoke this sentence
author.metaLine: 1873–1950 · Democratic congressman from Nebraska and monetary-reform campaigner
author.bio: Charles Gustav Binderup was born in Horsens, Denmark, brought to the United States as an infant, and worked as a farmer, merchant and realtor in Minden, Nebraska before representing Nebraska’s 4th district as a Democrat in the U.S. House from 1935 to 1939. He was a committed monetary reformer who helped organize the Constitutional Money League of America, and he used the House floor to argue that the Federal Reserve had deliberately engineered the 1920 downturn. Quotation researchers treat him as an unreliable conduit: he is also the figure credited with popularizing the debunked “Colonial Scrip” story about Benjamin Franklin and the Bank of England.

cite.sourceCitation: Charles G. Binderup, remarks in the U.S. House of Representatives, 19 March 1937, Congressional Record—House, vol. 81, pt. 3, p. 2528. misattribution.heading: How the line travelled
misattribution.intro: This is a quotation with no speaker — only a chain of people repeating what they believed someone else had said. Three different men have been named as its author, and the primary evidence supports none of them.

items.why: Every located instance is second-hand. The earliest, Binderup’s 1937 House speech, prefaces it with “It was Henry Ford who said, in substance, this” ↗ — a paraphrase, by the speaker’s own admission. Wikiquote lists it as misattributed ↗.

By 1974 The American Mercury was reporting that Jackson said, in his veto message, that “if the people only understood the rank injustice of our money and banking system there would be a revolution before morning” — a claim recorded in the ADS-L survey of the saying ↗. The full text of Jackson’s 1832 Bank veto message ↗ contains neither phrase, and Wikiquote’s Jackson page ↗ does not carry the line at all.

Monetary-conspiracy sites have also pinned the “revolution before morning” line on the Second Bank’s president in 1836 — a version quoted and flagged as needing “discovery and disclosure” on the ADS-L list ↗. No primary evidence has been produced.

The sentence people share today — “It is well enough that people of the nation do not understand…” — is not Binderup’s 1937 text. Goodreads carries this exact modern wording under Ford’s name with no source at all ↗, noting only that quotes are added by users and are not verified.

misattribution.truthLine: There is no documented occasion on which Henry Ford said or wrote this. The oldest text anyone has found is a Nebraska congressman’s paraphrase, delivered on the House floor on 19 March 1937 and printed at page 2528 of the Congressional Record ↗.

context.heading: Ford really did attack the banks — just never like this
lead: Henry Ford was a loud and public critic of finance, so the quotation feels right, and that is exactly why it has survived. But his actual published position is conspicuously cooler than the sentence pinned to him. In My Life and Work (1922), written with Samuel Crowther, Ford opens his money chapter by disclaiming exactly the posture the quotation gives him ↗: he says his objection to bankers has nothing to do with personalities, that he is not against bankers as such, that the world cannot go on without banking facilities — and only then asks whether credit has been built on the right foundation. Nowhere in that book does he predict a revolution.

The revolutionary version enters the record in 1937, on the floor of the House, in the middle of a speech alleging that the Federal Reserve secretly drained two billion dollars from circulation in 1920. Binderup’s own rhetoric immediately before it — that there would be “a change before morning if the people only knew” — is so close in shape to the sentence he then hands to Ford that the two are hard to separate. From there the line drifted through newspaper letters columns, congressional testimony and monetary-reform pamphlets, losing words and gaining polish, until it was reassigned outright to Andrew Jackson.
detailsBody: 19 March 1937 — Rep. Charles Binderup, Congressional Record—House vol. 81, p. 2528: “It was Henry Ford who said, in substance, this: ‘It is perhaps well enough that the people of the Nation do not know or understand our banking and monetary system, for if they did I believe there would be a revolution before tomorrow morning.’” The speech was reprinted in Father Coughlin’s weekly Social Justice the following month, per Ken Hirsch’s posting to the American Dialect Society list ↗.
11 October 1938 — a letter in the Hartford Courant gives a looser form: Ford supposedly said “There would be a revolution overnight if the people understood it.”
26 August 1941 — a letter to the Miami Daily News credits Ford with saying there would be “a revolution over night” if people knew the skulduggery of high finance.

1958 — Brig. Gen. Herbert C. Holdridge (ret.) puts a further variant into House Ways and Means hearings: “If the American people knew the corruption of our monetary system there would be a revolution before morning.”
1974 — The American Mercury transfers the saying to Andrew Jackson and claims he made it “in his veto message.” The 1938–1974 chain is documented in Garson O’Toole’s 2011 survey on the same list ↗.
